claims.text: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr–V-rich precipitates at approximately 8 dpa.
Irradiation increases the hardness of nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The baseline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy has overall radiation resistance.
The baseline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is currently manufacturable.
Replacing part of the Cr with 4–8 at% Hf will suppress irradiation-induced Cr–V-rich precipitates near 8 dpa.
The proposed example changes W38Ta36Cr15V11 to W38Ta32Cr11V11Hf8.
The Hf-modified alloy can be fabricated by standard powder-metallurgy or casting methods.
Thermomechanical processing can produce a nanocrystalline state in the proposed Hf-modified alloy.
Hf addition creates local lattice distortion in the modified alloy.
Hf addition produces Hf-based clusters in the modified alloy.
Hf-based clusters preferentially bind or tie up Cr and V atoms.
Hf-induced lattice distortion and clustering reduce the irradiation-driven mobility of Cr and V.
Reduced Cr and V mobility kinetically inhibits their segregation into precipitates.
Inhibiting Cr and V precipitation maintains a supersaturated solid solution.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain a homogeneous nanocrystalline BCC microstructure.
The Hf-modified alloy will exhibit post-irradiation hardness comparable to the unmodified nanocrystalline alloy.
The Hf modification will preserve practical bulk manufacturability.
Keeping the specimen below 600 °C, preferably below 500 °C, will limit thermally activated diffusion during irradiation.
The proposed hypothesis is limited to irradiation doses up to approximately 8 dpa.
Preliminary observations from related alloys support a beneficial role for minor Hf additions.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as replacing Cr with Hf, but the explicit example W38Ta32Cr11V11Hf8 reduces both Ta and Cr by 4 at% and adds 8 at% Hf. A true 8 at% substitution solely for Cr would instead retain Ta at 36 at% and reduce Cr to 7 at%.

The initial-state and baseline fields state that the unmodified alloy undergoes increased or associated hardening, whereas the predicted outcome defines success as maintaining low hardness comparable to that same unmodified alloy. The reference hardness state—unirradiated baseline, irradiated baseline, or negligible hardening—is not consistently specified.
